explanations.explanation: Judah it is, friend. Verses 1 and 2 just read off the twelve names like a roll call. Then verse 3 slows way down: “The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, and Shelah.” That's the list telling you which road it's taking.

Reuben does come first in the roll call of verse 1, so I see the pull. But in these verses he's only a name, same as the other eleven. The list slows down in verse 3, and it's Judah's sons it stops to name. Grabbing the first name in line is a very human move, and I'd have done it too.

Joseph shows up in verse 2, sitting between Dan and Benjamin. That's all he gets in this stretch, just a spot in the roll call. The list stops to name sons in verse 3, and those are Judah's sons. Joseph's a famous name, so I understand why it jumped out at you.

Wicked is the word, friend. Verse 3 says Er, Judah's firstborn, “…was wicked in the sight of the LORD. So the LORD put him to death.” That's a heavy line, so I'm not going to joke on it. I think the list stops for it because it's a sentence nobody can skim past.

Faithful is the opposite of what the text says. Verse 3 says Er “…was wicked in the sight of the LORD.” Then it says the LORD put him to death. It's a heavy verse, so I'll keep it plain: the text's word for Er is wicked.
Blameless is a good word, but it isn't the one in this verse. The text says Er “…was wicked in the sight of the LORD.” It's a heavy line, and the word the text gives us is wicked.

Tamar it is. Verse 4 says, “Tamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law, bore to him Perez and Zerah.” So the first three sons came by Bath-shua the Canaanite, and these two came by Tamar. Two mothers, five boys, and I bet that house was never quiet.

Rahab of Jericho is a real name in Scripture, and she's the woman who hid Israel's two spies (Joshua 2:1-4). But she isn't in this list. Verse 4 names Judah's daughter-in-law, Tamar, as the mother of Perez and Zerah. Different woman, friend.

Zipporah is the wife Moses, Israel's leader, was given in Midian (Exodus 2:21). She doesn't show up anywhere in this list. Verse 4 says Judah's daughter-in-law, Tamar, bore Perez and Zerah. Zipporah has a story of her own, and it's with Moses.
True. Er, Onan and Shelah came by Bath-shua, Perez and Zerah came by Tamar, and verse 4 wraps it up: “Judah had five sons in all.” Five sons, two mothers, and zero quiet mornings, I bet.

The text really says five. Verse 4 ends with “Judah had five sons in all.” Er, Onan and Shelah make three, and Perez and Zerah bring it to five. A list this full of names makes you want to double check the math, and I did too.

Leader is the word. Verse 10 calls Nahshon “…a leader of the descendants of Judah.” Most names around him just get a quick "father of" and move on. Nahshon gets a title, and that earns him a little extra spotlight.

Priest would be a fair guess in a list like this, but it isn't what the verse says. Verse 10 calls Nahshon “…a leader of the descendants of Judah.” He's out front of Judah's family, and the text gives him no other title.

Scribes do show up later in this chapter, in verse 55, with “…the clans of the scribes who lived at Jabez…” But that's way down the list and it's about clans, not Nahshon. Back in verse 10 the word for him is “…a leader of the descendants of Judah.” Easy to carry a word forward after this many names.

Boaz it is. Verse 11 says “…Salmon was the father of Boaz.” This is the Boaz whose field Ruth, the Moabite (Ruth 1:22), went to glean in (Ruth 2:3). After a wall of names, a face you know feels like spotting a friend at a crowded family reunion.

Elimelech was the husband of Naomi in the book of Ruth (Ruth 1:2). He belongs to Ruth's story, so I get the mix-up, but he isn't in this list. Verse 11 says “…Salmon was the father of Boaz.” Boaz is the man whose field Ruth went to (Ruth 2:3).

Mahlon was one of Elimelech's two sons in the book of Ruth (Ruth 1:2). He's tied to that story, but he isn't named here. Verse 11 says “…Salmon was the father of Boaz.” Ruth's book has a few men with similar vibes, so I don't blame you.
Jesse. Verse 12 says “…Obed was the father of Jesse.” And Jesse is the dad of seven sons, with David at the end of that line. We just walked up to the front door of David's house.
Kish was the father of Saul, who became king (1 Samuel 9:1-2; 11:15). That's a different family from this one. Verse 12 says “…Obed was the father of Jesse.” Different tree, friend.

Elkanah was the husband of Hannah, and Hannah bore their son Samuel (1 Samuel 1:1-2, 19-20). He's a real name from a real family, but not this one. Verse 12 says “…Obed was the father of Jesse.” Jesse is the name that fits in this line.
David, seventh and last on the list of Jesse's sons. Verse 15 finishes with “…and David seventh.” Seven names in order, and he's the one this whole list has been heading toward since Judah.
Ozem is sixth, right before the last spot. Verse 15 says “Ozem sixth, and David seventh.” Ozem got the position right before the big name, which is a tough spot for anybody.
Raddai is fifth, with Nethanel fourth in verse 14. That puts him two spots from the end. Verse 15 gives sixth to Ozem and seventh to David. Counting down a list this long takes patience, friend.

Nephew is it. Verse 16 says Zeruiah is David's sister, and Joab is her son. So David is Joab's uncle, and Joab is David's nephew. Joab ends up leading David's army (2 Samuel 8:16), so I bet family gatherings had some interesting seating.

Cousin would mean Joab's parent is a brother or sister of David's parent. But Joab's mother, Zeruiah, is David's own sister (verse 16). That puts Joab one step closer than a cousin. Closer than cousin means nephew.
Uncle flips it around. Zeruiah is David's sister (verse 16), so her son Joab is David's nephew. In this pair, David's the uncle. I'd flip them too after that many names in a row.

Amasa is the one. Verse 17 says, “Abigail was the mother of Amasa, whose father was Jether the Ishmaelite.” Since Abigail is David's sister (verse 16), Amasa is another nephew of David's. Two sisters, two sets of nephews, and a lot of cousins at one table.

Abishai is one of Zeruiah's three sons (verse 16), not Abigail's. Zeruiah and Abigail are the sisters, and their sons can get tangled. Verse 17 gives Abigail's son: Amasa, whose father was Jether the Ishmaelite.

Asahel is the third of Zeruiah's sons (verse 16), so he's her boy, not Abigail's. Verse 17 says Abigail was the mother of Amasa, whose father was Jether the Ishmaelite. Two sisters in a row, and I'd need a notepad too.

Not quite, friend. Verse 1 says Amnon's mother is Ahinoam of Jezreel. Daniel, the second son, is by Abigail of Carmel. That's two different mothers, and this Abigail isn't David's sister Abigail from earlier in the list.

False, and you caught it. Amnon was born by Ahinoam of Jezreel, and Daniel by Abigail of Carmel (verse 1). Watch the name: this Abigail isn't David's sister Abigail from earlier in the list. Same name, different woman.

King Talmai of Geshur is the answer. Verse 2 says “…Absalom the son of Maacah daughter of King Talmai of Geshur…” So Absalom's grandfather on his mother's side is a king. Not a bad name to drop at a family gathering.

Hiram was a king who sent cedar logs and builders to David (2 Samuel 5:11). He's a real king in David's story, but he's not Maacah's father. Verse 2 names Talmai of Geshur for that. Good king guess, wrong king, friend.

Achish was the king of Gath, where David once fled from Saul (1 Samuel 21:10). He's in David's story, but not in this list. Verse 2 says Maacah is the daughter of King Talmai of Geshur. Plenty of kings in David's life, so it's easy to mix them up.

About forty is right. Verse 4 gives seven years and six months in Hebron plus thirty-three years in Jerusalem. That adds up to forty and a half. Forty and a half years on one job, which is longer than most of us stay anywhere.
Thirty is close to the Jerusalem number, but that one's thirty-three. It also leaves out the seven years and six months in Hebron. Add them together and you get forty and a half, so about forty.

Fifty overshoots it. Verse 4 gives seven years and six months in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem. Together that's forty and a half, which is about forty. Fifty would add nearly ten years the text doesn't give.

Solomon, David's son, is the answer. Verse 5 lists Shimea, Shobab, Nathan and Solomon, and says, “These four were born to him by Bathsheba daughter of Ammiel.” Solomon's son Rehoboam then starts the next stretch in verse 10.
Absalom is David's third son, born in Hebron to Maacah (verses 1-2). Bathsheba's four were born in Jerusalem (verse 5). Different city, different mother. Even I'd need a chart for this one.

Amnon is David's firstborn, born in Hebron to Ahinoam of Jezreel (verse 1). Bathsheba's four were born in Jerusalem: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan and Solomon (verse 5). Amnon came well before them. Watch the cities and the list sorts out the order for you.

Tamar. Verse 9 says, “And Tamar was their sister.” It's the same name as Judah's daughter-in-law from way back in chapter 2, but this one is a sister to David's sons. Two women, one name, and a list that doesn't stop to clear it up for us.

Michal was the daughter of Saul, and Saul gave her to David as a wife (1 Samuel 18:27). So she's David's wife, not a sister to his sons. Verse 9 says, “And Tamar was their sister.” I get why a famous name came to mind.
Merab was Saul's older daughter (1 Samuel 18:17). She isn't named in this list. Verse 9 says, “And Tamar was their sister.” Lots of daughters in David's world, so it's easy to grab the wrong name.

True. Verse 10 starts with Solomon's son Rehoboam, then says, “Abijah was his son, Asa his son…” and keeps that up through verse 14. It's a straight father-to-son line. Like a relay race where nobody drops the baton.

The text says it's true. Verse 10 says, “Abijah was his son, Asa his son…” and it keeps going all the way to Josiah in verse 14. Every name is the son of the one before him. No cousin sneaks in the middle.
Josiah. Verse 14 closes the run with “Amon his son, and Josiah his son.” After that, the list moves on to Josiah's own sons in verse 15.
Omri became king of Israel (1 Kings 16:23), but he isn't in this line of names. Verse 14 says Amon's son is Josiah. Omri belongs to another family tree.
Ahab was Omri's son, and he became king of Israel (1 Kings 16:28-29). He isn't in this list. Verse 14 ends with “…and Josiah his son.” In this list, Amon's son is Josiah.
Captive. Verse 17 says “The descendants of Jeconiah the captive…” That one word fits with Jeconiah being carried away to Babylon (Jeremiah 24:1). One word, and it tells you where he ended up.

The verse doesn't call Jeconiah a prophet. It says, “The descendants of Jeconiah the captive…” Jeremiah 24:1 says he was carried away to Babylon. A prophet speaks for God, and the text gives Jeconiah a different title.

Priest is a title the list never gives Jeconiah. Verse 17 says, “The descendants of Jeconiah the captive…” He was carried away to Babylon (Jeremiah 24:1). It's captive, and that's the word the list uses for him.

Not so, friend. Verse 17 says Jeconiah's descendants start with “Shealtiel his son,” and the list keeps going. Zerubbabel comes in verse 19, and it runs down to Elioenai's seven sons in verse 24. A captive with a long family line behind him.
False, and good catch. The list doesn't stop with Jeconiah. It says, “Shealtiel his son,” then moves on through Zerubbabel and keeps going until verse 24. The captive's family tree isn't done.
